question: If AI agents can help find new things in science, how do we make sure people still check and understand the results?
reflection: When machines search faster and scientists test with care, discoveries can reach the people who need them sooner.

sources.subject: 950 Claude Agents Ran Overnight and Rewrote Biology's Rulebook

one_line: AI agents report a first biology discovery, while US lawmakers propose banning superintelligence and tech leaders warn the UN.

top_stories.title: Hundreds of AI agents flag a new enzyme system
top_stories.what: Anthropic says about 950 Claude agents searched a DNA database for 21 hours and flagged a previously undescribed enzyme system, which scientists then tested in the lab.
top_stories.why: Agents that screen huge datasets and hand promising leads to experts could speed up research in health and other fields.

top_stories.title: US bill would ban superintelligence
top_stories.what: Two US lawmakers proposed a bill to permanently ban building artificial superintelligence, pause advanced AI work and create a new federal AI department.
top_stories.why: Even if it does not pass, the bill shows how far the political debate on AI risk has moved, which affects global policy talks.

top_stories.title: Daily AI users are still worried
top_stories.what: A Gallup survey reportedly found that 68% of Americans who use AI every day are concerned about its effects.
top_stories.why: Heavy use alongside high worry is a classic behavioural gap, useful for designing trust and communication programmes.

saudi_lens.text: Agent-led screening of genetic data could support Saudi genomics and biotech research, provided that data governance and lab validation stay in local hands.

idea.title: Use and worry survey
idea.pitch: Measure how often people use AI tools and what worries them, to find groups that use AI a lot but trust it little.
idea.first_step: Draft a short survey pairing usage questions with five common worries, and test it with ten people.

idea_kids.title: Pattern hunters
idea_kids.pitch: A hands-on activity where children search long printed strings of coloured beads or letters for a repeating pattern, like scientists searching DNA.
idea_kids.first_step: Prepare five bead strings, each hiding one repeating pattern, and a simple record sheet.
